units.source_excerpt: The shape of a snowboarding halfpipe can be designed to maximize the vertical air a professional snowboarder will achieve; however, a practical course will take into account factors such as the number of cycles and the shape that yields the best launch for stunts.
units.function: Open with the mathematical objective and immediately bound it by practical performance criteria.
units.reusable_pattern: {Object} can be designed to maximize {primary metric}; however, a practical {system} must also account for {secondary criteria}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call the practical criteria optimized unless an explicit decision rule evaluates them.

units.source_excerpt: As a snowboarder descends a halfpipe the forces acting on him are dependent on the shape of the course. We will use Newton's Second Law of Motion to sum the forces in each direction. Then we used a Runge-Kutta method computer simulation to determine the acceleration.
units.function: Compress the causal geometry-to-force-to-solver chain into reader order.

features.quantitative_role: names the governing law and integrator

units.reusable_pattern: Because {mechanism} depends on {design variable}, sum {forces} by {law}; then solve {state equations} with {method}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not let naming a numerical method stand in for equation or code validation.

units.source_excerpt: We tested three different functions that describe the shape of the half pipe, with three varying slopes for each.
units.function: State the candidate family and factorial comparison compactly.
units.reusable_pattern: We tested {n} {candidate forms}, with {m} {control settings} for each.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not imply a fair shape comparison unless depth, width, endpoint angle, and event definitions are aligned.

units.source_excerpt: The forces taken into consideration in these models include: gravity, centrifugal, frictional, air resistance, and a constant force applied in the direction of travel that mimics the force from a professional snowboarder pumping his legs.
units.function: Inventory included mechanisms before stating the excluded control behavior.
units.reusable_pattern: The model includes {mechanism list} and represents {active effect} as {proxy}; it does not represent {excluded behavior}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call an included term operational when its parameter is absent from the executed code.

units.source_excerpt: After running our three models we determined that out of the various shapes tested the best vertical height was optimized at a mountain slope of 45 degrees with a half pipe shape of the parabola z(y)=.07y^2-7.
units.function: Place the selected configuration and its literal geometry in the abstract.
units.reusable_pattern: Across the tested {candidate set}, {configuration} produced the largest {reported response}; its defining equation is {equation}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not replace a conditional tested-set ranking with a universal optimum.

units.source_excerpt: The best practical model was found to be the same parabola at a mountain slope of 25 degrees. The Runge Kutta method approximation had an error of 0.1%. Our best model is the comprehensive three dimensional force model because it most realistically describes a snowboarder on a halfpipe.
units.function: Close with a practical configuration, numerical-method claim, and preferred model level.
units.reusable_pattern: For {practical criterion}, select {configuration}; report {numerical diagnostic}; prefer {model level} because it adds {named mechanism}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not imitate the 0.1 percent claim without a reference solution and norm; do not equate more dimensions with realism by assertion.

units.source_excerpt: Developed in the 1970's, snowboarding has come a long way from the original snurfer (snow-surfer) which was an attempt by Shermann Poppen to bring surfing to the Rocky Mountains.
units.function: Enter the technical problem through a compact domain-history hook.

features.clause_structure: participial opener plus historical relative clause

units.reusable_pattern: Developed in {period}, {domain object} evolved from {origin} into {current performance setting}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not spend domain-history space that does not narrow toward the modeled object.

units.source_excerpt: For this problem we will look specifically at the half-pipe in order to optimize vertical air.
units.function: Narrow from the broad sport to the exact design object and objective.
units.reusable_pattern: For this problem, we focus on {literal object} in order to optimize {metric}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use a broad domain label where a literal modeled object is available.

units.source_excerpt: vertical air which can be defined as the distance a skilled snowboarder can obtain by being launched off the edge of the halfpipe
units.function: Operationally define the judged performance phrase at first use.

features.clause_structure: noun phrase plus defining relative clause

units.reusable_pattern: Define {domain term} as {measured quantity} relative to {reference event or surface}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not later substitute exit velocity for the defined distance without an explicit flight handoff.

units.source_excerpt: A basic halfpipe consists of two concave ramps separated by a distance which totals to the width of the half pipe. The vertical side is called a vertical, the curved part is called the transition, and the distance between the two ramps is called the flat.
units.function: Decompose the facility and establish a shared component vocabulary before equations.
units.reusable_pattern: A {system} consists of {components}; call {part A} the {term A}, {part B} the {term B}, and {gap} the {term C}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not change component names between geometry, equations, figures, and code.

units.source_excerpt: The vertical and transition allow for back and forth motion using gravity to give the snowboarder a velocity. A snowboarder uses the flat to regain balance as well as a time to pump. Pumping adds work to the system.
units.function: Map each physical component to its performance role and energy mechanism.
units.reusable_pattern: Use {component} for {motion role}; during {phase}, {action} adds {energy or impulse} to the system.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not describe added work without specifying direction, duration, and implementation.

units.source_excerpt: A snowboarding halfpipe is a basic halfpipe that is built onto a hill. The slope of the hill gives a new form of energy that can be converted to velocity and used to maximize vertical air.
units.function: Introduce the real-course extension by naming the one added geometry and its intended energy pathway.
units.reusable_pattern: Extend the baseline {object} by adding {geometric feature}; this introduces {energy or force pathway} into {performance output}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim conversion into the target metric until coordinate and flight transformations are explicit.

units.source_excerpt: The higher the vertical the more difficult it is to land while a narrow stretch between the two verticals provides less time to recover as well as less opportunity to pump.
units.function: Translate geometry choices into opposing performance and safety consequences.
units.reusable_pattern: Increasing {geometry A} improves {benefit} but worsens {cost}, while decreasing {geometry B} reduces {recovery or control margin}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not convert qualitative tradeoffs into a practical optimum without weights or constraints.

units.source_excerpt: So what is the best shape of a half pipe to optimize a skilled snowboarder's vertical air? And what kind of options does the snowboarder have for a variety of stunts? And what changes could be made to develop a practical course?
units.function: Close the analysis with a three-question contract spanning optimum, alternate performance, and practicality.
units.reusable_pattern: Ask in order: which {design} maximizes {primary output}; what supports {secondary output}; what changes make the design practical?
prohibited_generalizations: Do not let later sections silently drop the secondary or practical question.

units.source_excerpt: In order to find a snowboarder's optimized vertical air we used both conservation of energy and Newton's 2nd Law to account for the various forces acting on a snowboarder while traveling down the half-pipe.
units.function: Connect the objective to two complementary physical formalisms.
units.reusable_pattern: To evaluate {objective}, combine {baseline law} with {dynamic law} so that {mechanisms} enter the same account.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not list laws without stating what distinct role each performs.

units.source_excerpt: Using a function z(y) for the shape of the halfpipe we were able to set up a model that allows a function to be easily altered and evaluated for any shape.
units.function: Declare a replaceable mathematical interface for candidate geometry.
units.reusable_pattern: Represent {design object} by {function}; keep the solver unchanged while substituting and evaluating {candidate family}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim arbitrary-shape support unless geometry derivatives and branches are total.

units.source_excerpt: Conservation of Energy Model; Two Dimensional Force Model; Comprehensive Three Dimensional Force Model.
units.function: Give the reader three stable labels that encode the escalation before derivation.
units.reusable_pattern: Preview a named ladder: {baseline model}; {mechanism model}; {higher-dimensional extension}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use 'comprehensive' as evidence that every required mechanism or output is present.

units.source_excerpt: The conservation of energy model is our most intuitive analysis of the snowboarders speed. Looking at the conversion of potential energy to a new potential energy we can determine analytically the kinetic energy used to launch a snowboarder.
units.function: Begin with the most intuitive model and name exactly what it can determine analytically.
units.reusable_pattern: Begin with {intuitive baseline}; through {conservation relation}, determine {analytic output} before adding losses or controls.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not make the baseline responsible for mechanisms it intentionally omits.

units.source_excerpt: KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f. Under the following conditions: v_i=0, h_i>h_f. The conservation of energy results in v=sqrt(2g(h_i-h_f)).
units.function: Place conditions immediately between the governing balance and its reduced formula.
units.reusable_pattern: State {governing balance}; under {conditions}, reduce it to {decision-facing formula}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not hide initial or boundary conditions in prose far from the reduction.

units.source_excerpt: Without adding any work the snowboarder will never go beyond the original height. In order to see the importance of pumping we added work to the system and the equation of velocity is changed by a factor of work.
units.function: Use an impossibility result from the baseline to motivate the active-work modification.
units.reusable_pattern: Without {mechanism}, {baseline limit}; therefore add {mechanism} and show its exact term in {updated equation}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not reuse the printed active-work formula without restoring dimensional consistency.

units.source_excerpt: A higher velocity means there is a higher vertical air. However, the angle of take off must be taken into account as well. When theta=pi/2 our velocity is entirely in the z direction; when theta=0 our velocity is entirely in the x direction.
units.function: Qualify a magnitude-based result by decomposing direction through two limiting angles.

features.clause_structure: claim plus however plus paired limits

units.reusable_pattern: {Magnitude} affects {output}; however, direction matters: at {limit A}, {component A}; at {limit B}, {component B}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not infer a practical optimum from a component maximum without clearance and landing constraints.

units.source_excerpt: The information provided by this analysis gives an intuitive look into what a snowboarder's motion would be neglecting all forms of friction in a two dimensional plane, with the option to add work.
units.function: Restate the output together with the exact idealizations that make it interpretable.
units.reusable_pattern: This analysis gives {interpretive output} under {dimension}, neglecting {omissions}, with {optional mechanism} treated separately.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not let an intuitive result migrate into the full model without rechecking its assumptions.

units.source_excerpt: Strengths: quick simulations, easy height changes, work can be added, and the path is unrestricted. Weaknesses: no optimal half-pipe or hill angle and no frictional forces.
units.function: Close the model rung with capability and omission lists that justify escalation.
units.reusable_pattern: After each model, list what it computes or varies, then list the omissions that the next model is designed to repair.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not substitute a weakness inventory for learning the positive organization of the model rung.

units.source_excerpt: In order to model a snowboarder's path down a two dimensional movement we used a set of ordinary differential equations for the forces acting on the snowboarder in both z and y directions.
units.function: Open the second rung by naming the state directions, equation family, and included forces.
units.reusable_pattern: To model {path}, write {equation family} in {state directions} and resolve {force inventory} along those axes.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call nonlinear force equations linear ODEs.

units.source_excerpt: Using Newton's Second Law of Motion, sum F=ma, we can see that the force acting on the snowboarder in the y-axis is equal to mass times acceleration. Applying this to both the y and z axis yields two second order differential equations.
units.function: Bridge the vector law to component equations before numerical conversion.
units.reusable_pattern: Apply {vector law} along {axes} to obtain {component equations}; then rewrite them as {solver state form}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not switch between force and acceleration notation without a mass-normalization crosswalk.

units.source_excerpt: Using a computer simulated Runge-Kutta method, the four differential equations are solved yielding the snowboarder's path and velocity across the halfpipe.
units.function: Name the numerical handoff from first-order states to path and velocity outputs.

features.quantitative_role: four equations and two output types

units.reusable_pattern: Solve the {n} first-order equations with {integrator}, yielding {trajectory} and {state outputs}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not equate a named integrator with validated derivatives or stable constraints.

units.source_excerpt: This model shows how different shapes affect the amount of energy lost due to friction and drag. With the added force being constant, and the dimensions similar, each shape can be analyzed side by side.
units.function: Explain the comparison mechanism and state the intended controls for side-by-side ranking.
units.reusable_pattern: Compare {candidates} through {loss mechanism}, holding {active input} and {geometry controls} fixed.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not describe dimensions as similar when the tested depths and endpoint slopes differ materially.

units.source_excerpt: In order to model this problem in three dimensions we came up with a three dimensional force diagram. We are taking into account the zx plane's potential energy that is being converted into kinetic energy as the snowboarder descends the hill.
units.function: Open the third rung with the added plane and its intended energy pathway.
units.reusable_pattern: Extend {lower-dimensional model} by adding {plane or coordinate}; show which {energy or force pathway} becomes representable.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call the extension comprehensive before output coordinates and coupled losses are reconciled.

units.source_excerpt: For the sake of simplicity we shifted the axis used to define the zx plane so that the normal force is solely in the z direction. An important observation is the fact that we redefined the coordinate system.
units.function: Pair a coordinate simplification with an explicit warning that downstream gravity components change.
units.reusable_pattern: Rotate {coordinate frame} to align {force}; immediately state how this changes {gravity, velocity, and output components}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not compare rotated components with global vertical distance without transforming them back.

units.source_excerpt: With the force caused by the ramp going down a slope added, this model allows the path and velocity of the snowboarder side to side to be evaluated as well as the velocity down the hill.
units.function: State the new model output in direct contrast with the lower-dimensional rung.
units.reusable_pattern: Adding {force or coordinate} expands the output from {old outputs} to {new output set}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not say the expanded state computes the official target unless the target equation is present.

units.source_excerpt: This model allows different combinations of slope and cross-sectionals to be tested together. It does not take into account how a professional snowboarder will guide his path down the halfpipe.
units.function: Close the ladder by pairing combinatorial design scope with the missing human-control mechanism.
units.reusable_pattern: The extension permits joint testing of {design variables}, but excludes {control behavior}; keep recommendations conditional on that boundary.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not narrate unmodeled rider control as if it were an output of the model.

units.source_excerpt: The snowboarder does not add force to the system causing a change in direction.
units.function: Bound the human controller by excluding steering force.
units.reusable_pattern: Assume {actor} does not apply {control input} that changes {state direction}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not invoke the excluded control later to justify a recommendation.

units.source_excerpt: The force added in the two-dimensional model to mimic the snowboarder pumping his legs was added by adding a single constant force in the direction of travel.
units.function: Declare the simplified active-force proxy with magnitude behavior and direction.
units.reusable_pattern: Represent {human action} by {bounded proxy}, applied with {magnitude behavior} in {direction and phase}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat an uncalibrated constant as measured athlete behavior.

units.source_excerpt: In the three-dimensional model the added force is only taken into consideration in the z-y plane. No projectile motion is modeled for after the snowboarder leaves the halfpipe.
units.function: Close assumptions with spatial and downstream-process boundaries.

features.quantitative_role: limits force plane and time horizon

units.reusable_pattern: Apply {input} only in {subspace}; terminate the model at {event}, with {downstream phase} explicitly omitted.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not later claim the omitted downstream phase was verified or optimized.

units.source_excerpt: After evaluating each model we came to the conclusion that the best model is the three dimensional force model. Both the conservation model and the two dimensional force model are necessary for evaluating how the slope changes velocity and demonstrating pumping.
units.function: Open results by selecting the reporting model while preserving the explanatory role of earlier rungs.
units.reusable_pattern: Use {full model} for final comparison, while retaining {baseline models} for {specific interpretive checks}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not rank a model as best solely because it has more dimensions.

units.source_excerpt: This was an analytical model so there is no data to graph. However, a clear understanding of the model gives an intuitive look into why we choose to use second order differential equations to model the more complex systems.
units.function: Report a non-graphical result by stating its explanatory handoff to the next model.
units.reusable_pattern: Because {baseline} is analytic, report {derived insight} rather than a plot; use that insight to motivate {next model}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not manufacture a graph when the analytical result itself is the evidence.

units.source_excerpt: The two dimensional force model is used to evaluate the final velocity at the peak of the opposite vertical. By breaking the velocity into y and z components we were able to compare the final z velocity of three different functions.
units.function: Define the comparison event, decompose the output, and name the ranking component before the table.

features.quantitative_role: y and z components for three candidates

units.reusable_pattern: At {comparison event}, decompose {vector output} into {components}; rank {candidate set} using {named component or scalar metric}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not switch from one component to vector magnitude without naming the scalar objective.

units.source_excerpt: Shape Name and Formula: Parabola 1 z(y)=.07y^2-7; Parabola 2 z(y)=.1y^2-10; Circle z(y)=sqrt(100-y^2).
units.function: Place literal candidate equations beside the first numeric comparison.
units.reusable_pattern: Beside the result table, key each {candidate name} to its exact {equation and domain}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not compare shape families without listing their depths, domains, and endpoint slopes.

units.source_excerpt: Figure 4: Displacement in the YZ Plane. Figure 5: Displacement in the YZ Plane Adding Work.
units.function: Use matched before-and-after figure labels to isolate the narrative effect of active work.
units.reusable_pattern: Pair {baseline figure} with {same view plus one declared modification}; keep axes and scales aligned.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim a controlled effect when the code does not implement the declared modification.

units.source_excerpt: By comparing and contrasting the three different models we can extrapolate that: Parabola 1 is 23 percent better than parabola 2; Parabola 2 is 1.6 percent better than the circle.
units.function: Close the two-dimensional comparison with a compact ranked quantitative list.
units.reusable_pattern: From {named metric}, report pairwise differences as {A versus B, numerator, denominator}; then state the conditional ranking.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not imitate the printed 23 percent without naming and checking its denominator.

units.source_excerpt: The comprehensive three dimensional force model allows the displacement in the x, y and z direction to be graphed in a three dimensional graph. To evaluate the best halfpipe shape we again looked at the velocities at the top of the vertical point.
units.function: Preserve the same comparison event while expanding the displayed state dimensions.
units.reusable_pattern: In the expanded model, retain {same event and candidate set} while adding {new state components}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not ignore an added component if it affects the global target or event timing.

units.source_excerpt: At 45 degrees the table reports y and z velocities for Parabola 1, Parabola 2, and Circle, followed by pairwise statements about which shape is better for maximizing vertical air.
units.function: Attach interpretation directly beneath the unit-bearing multi-component table.
units.reusable_pattern: Under {fixed setting}, present {unit-bearing component table}; immediately state the scalar metric and conditional comparison.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not reproduce the paper's reversed Parabola 1 versus Parabola 2 prose ranking.

units.source_excerpt: In the conservation of energy model vertical air is maximized when the takeoff angle is closest to 90 degrees; the two-dimensional model selects z=.07y^2-7; the comprehensive model selects that parabola at a slope of 45 degrees.
units.function: Synthesize one decision by walking through the three model rungs in body order.
units.reusable_pattern: Triangulate the decision: {baseline} establishes {criterion}; {mechanism model} selects {geometry}; {full model} selects {control setting}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call the triangulation complete when the requested flight distance is absent.

units.source_excerpt: This is what the model tells us is the best shape but the model does not take into account that a snowboarder has various techniques to convert velocities in one direction to another such as carving and toe turns.
units.function: Interrupt the maximum recommendation with the omitted human-control mechanism.
units.reusable_pattern: The model selects {choice}, but omits {control mechanism}; therefore interpret the choice only under {fixed behavior}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use the omitted control immediately afterward as evidence for another optimum.

units.source_excerpt: When applying this model to a more realistic situation where a snowboarder converts most of the x-velocity into side to side velocity, we might reevaluate this conclusion.
units.function: Open the practical branch by changing the behavioral scenario and signaling reevaluation.
units.reusable_pattern: For the practical branch, change {behavioral scenario}; reevaluate {maximum choice} under {new criterion}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call a scenario more realistic without evidence or calibrated behavior.

units.source_excerpt: It is the same parabola with a different mountain slope of 25 degrees that gives the best realistic shape for a half pipe.
units.function: Close with a minimally changed practical configuration that is easy to compare with the maximum.
units.reusable_pattern: Keep {geometry} fixed and change {control} from {maximum setting} to {practical setting}; state the practical criterion explicitly.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not imitate the practical label without safety, landing, cycle, and construction criteria.

units.source_excerpt: Physical testing for the two and three dimensional force models; computer simulation with known values; analytical testing for the conservation of energy model.
units.function: Preview three verification modes and assign each to the model rung it can test.
units.reusable_pattern: Map {physical test}, {computational check}, and {analytical limit} to the exact model claim each addresses.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not collapse illustrative, numerical, and analytical checks into one validation status.

units.source_excerpt: We were able to set up a physical model and send a marble down the halfpipe to verify that our computer simulations were modeling the system correctly. The path the marble followed almost exactly mirrored the three dimensional graph.
units.function: Turn an abstract trajectory into a tangible physical analogue and place it beside the simulation.
units.reusable_pattern: Build {scaled analogue}, observe {trajectory}, and place it beside {simulation view}; reserve validation language for registered residuals.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not imitate 'almost exactly mirrored' without scale, calibration, repeats, and error metrics.

units.source_excerpt: Taking away friction and drag and checking that the snowboarder continues perpetually in a pendulum-like motion; by not adding work and checking that the snowboarder continues with damped motion until coming to rest.
units.function: Use two opposite limiting cases to test conservative and dissipative behavior.
units.reusable_pattern: Check paired limits: with {losses removed}, recover {conservative behavior}; with {input removed}, recover {dissipative behavior}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call qualitative limit behavior a convergence or accuracy test.

units.source_excerpt: Setting phi equal to 0 and checking that the three dimensional model gave the same results as the two dimensional model under the same conditions.
units.function: Test the higher-dimensional model by recovering its nested lower-dimensional case.
units.reusable_pattern: Set {extension parameter}=0; under identical {inputs and events}, recover {baseline model outputs}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim nested recovery unless all other code paths and initial states are identical.

units.source_excerpt: The snowboarder only has as much energy as he starts with when no work is added; he would only be able to reach his original height. When adding work, pumping gives an additional force to the system.
units.function: Reapply the baseline energy invariant as an interpretive check on the dynamic model.
units.reusable_pattern: Use {analytic invariant} to check {solver}: under {zero input}, recover {bound}; with {input}, change only through {named term}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not accept a qualitative story when units in the added-work equation are inconsistent.

units.source_excerpt: For our two dimensional model, we computed the error in position due to the Runge Kutta approximation to be 0.1% with a delta t of 0.00001 iterated for 30 seconds.
units.function: Report the numerical claim together with step size, horizon, and affected state.
units.reusable_pattern: For {model}, report {error metric} against {reference}, using {step grid}, {horizon}, and {norm}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not reuse the 0.1 percent claim because the paper provides no reference solution, norm, or refinement table.

units.source_excerpt: It is possible to achieve less than 0.1% error by reducing our delta t; however for the given project 0.1% error is a very acceptable percentage.
units.function: Close numerical analysis with a refinement direction and decision tolerance statement.
units.reusable_pattern: Refining {numerical control} changes {error}; accept {tolerance} only because {decision} remains unchanged within a declared contract.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call a tolerance acceptable without showing convergence and its effect on the decision.

units.source_excerpt: A possible future model could be a half-pipe down the slope given by the equation of a cycloid. A cycloid is what Bernoulli found to be as the line of fastest descent.
units.function: Propose a named geometric extension and connect it to an established analytic property.
units.reusable_pattern: Extend {current geometry} to {named family} because it optimizes {related analytic property}; state the new objective and fixed constraints.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not transfer a fastest-descent theorem directly to vertical-air optimality.

units.source_excerpt: Realistically this would not necessarily be the best model as the slope of a mountain is rarely in the cycloid equation form.
units.function: Immediately bound the elegant extension by construction and terrain feasibility.
units.reusable_pattern: Although {candidate} has {analytic advantage}, it may be infeasible because {physical or construction constraint}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat analytic elegance as practical design evidence.

units.source_excerpt: Further testing with piecewise function as well as adding different types of work. Also, finding some way to take into account the stylistic choices of a skilled snowboarder would be another factor.
units.function: Convert three known omissions into a compact extension roadmap.
units.reusable_pattern: Extend along three axes: {geometry family}, {input model}, and {human or control behavior}; define evidence needed for each.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not leave future work as vague 'more testing' without variables and acceptance evidence.

units.source_excerpt: Parameters you may want to change: N, DELTA_T, T_MAX, initial states, m, g, mu, w, hi, rho_air, area, c_d, PI, and phi.
units.function: Expose the numerical and physical controls in one inspectable implementation block.
units.reusable_pattern: Before the solver, list {states}, {numerical controls}, {initial conditions}, and {physical parameters} with units and sources.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not assume a declared macro controls execution; trace every parameter to its use.

units.source_excerpt: Define the ODE: compute dz/dy, d2z/dy2, theta, drag, curvature radius, normal loading, force components, and return the derivative selected by state index.
units.function: Make the paper equation-to-code pathway inspectable at derivative level.
units.reusable_pattern: In one derivative function, map {geometry} to {orientation}, {forces}, and {state derivatives}; cross-reference every paper equation.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not imitate the branch implementation without fixing overwritten and uninitialized derivatives.

units.source_excerpt: Initialize y[0] from INITIAL_Y0, construct y[1] from the piecewise surface, set velocity states, then call runge4 in the time loop and print y[0], y[1], and y[5].
units.function: Expose the initial-state, event-loop, and output path that owns the result tables.
units.reusable_pattern: Show {all state initializations}, {termination event}, {integrator call}, and {printed outputs} in one traceable execution path.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not reuse the code without initializing y[4] and y[5] before the loop condition and output.

units.source_excerpt: The runge4 routine computes k1, k2, k3, and k4 at the two midpoint stages and endpoint, then updates each state by (k1+2k2+2k3+k4)/6.
units.function: Publish the recognizable numerical kernel rather than only naming it in prose.
units.reusable_pattern: After naming {integrator}, print the stage construction and final update so readers can verify the numerical kernel.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not infer model correctness merely because the RK4 kernel is recognizable.

units.source_excerpt: Figure 9 labels the wall, flat, transition, vertical, lip, deck, width, and height; Figure 10 places the basic halfpipe in x-y-z coordinates.
units.function: Reconnect code coordinates and geometry terms to the physical course.
units.reusable_pattern: Pair a {domain-labeled figure} with a {coordinate-labeled model figure} so every axis and surface term has a physical referent.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not leave coordinate orientation inferential when global vertical is the target.

units.source_excerpt: The appendix places color-coded velocity tables for shapes, slopes, and cycle numbers before a compact comprehensive-force equation summary, equations 15-21.
units.function: End the appendix by exposing scenario outputs and restating the governing symbols next to them.

features.clause_structure: scenario rows followed by displayed equations

units.reusable_pattern: Place {scenario table} beside a compact {equation and symbol recap}; link each column to a state and event definition.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not treat unexplained zero rows or mixed cycle events as comparable outcomes.
